title: COD — Hach Reactor Digestion (DR6000)
methodRef: Hach Method 8000 — Reactor Digestion; USEPA approved for wastewater reporting
instrument: Hach DR6000 Spectrophotometer with DRB200 reactor
hachMethod: Method 8000 — Reactor Digestion, using pre-dosed TNTplus or standard COD vials
range: Ultra-low 0.7–40 mg/L; low range 3–150 mg/L; high range 20–1500 mg/L; high range plus 250–15000 mg/L
sampleVolume: 2.00 mL into the vial (0.20 mL for high range plus)
wavelength: 420 nm (low range) / 620 nm (high range) — set automatically by the stored program
frequency: Daily on influent and effluent; per the discharge consent monitoring schedule
holdingTime: 28 days if preserved with sulfuric acid to pH < 2 and stored at 4 °C; otherwise analyse within 24 h
equipment: Hach DRB200 COD reactor preheated to 150 °C
COD vial adapter for the DR6000
Adjustable pipette, 2.00 mL, with clean tips
reagents: Hach COD digestion reagent vials of the appropriate range
Deionised water for the reagent blank
COD standard solution for QC verification
interferences: CHLORIDE is the major interference and is positively biasing — the mercuric sulfate in the vials complexes it, but samples above roughly 2000 mg/L chloride still need dilution or a chloride-tolerant vial.
A non-homogeneous sample gives poor duplicates — COD samples containing solids must be blended before pipetting.
Pipetting error is the largest source of variability, since only 2.00 mL is used. An inaccurate pipette directly scales the error.
Vials must be inverted to mix after adding sample or the digestion is incomplete.
steps: PREHEAT the DRB200 reactor to 150 °C and confirm it has reached temperature before starting. Digestion at a lower temperature gives low results.
Select the vial range appropriate to the expected COD. If the range is unknown, run the sample on high range first, then repeat on a narrower range if the result is low.
HOMOGENISE the sample thoroughly. For influent or any sample containing solids, blend it — an unblended sample makes the 2 mL aliquot unrepresentative and duplicates will not agree.
Verify the pipette's accuracy is within its calibration schedule. At 2.00 mL, a 2 % pipette error is a 2 % COD error.
PREPARE THE BLANK: pipette exactly 2.00 mL of deionised water into a COD vial of the same lot.
PREPARE THE SAMPLE: pipette exactly 2.00 mL of homogenised sample into a second vial, holding the vial at an angle to let the sample run down the wall.
Cap both vials tightly. Wipe the outside clean — spilled digestion reagent will damage the reactor and stain the vial optics.
INVERT each vial several times to mix. The vials become very hot during this step because of the acid dilution heat — hold them by the cap.
Place the vials in the preheated reactor and digest for exactly 120 minutes.
At the end of digestion, remove the vials and place them in a rack to cool to about 120 °C, then invert each one several times while still warm.
Cool the vials to room temperature in the rack. Do NOT quench them in water — thermal shock breaks vials and the result is affected by temperature.
Select the stored program for COD by the appropriate range on the DR6000, and fit the vial adapter.
Wipe each vial with a lint-free cloth. Fingerprints and residue on a round vial are a major source of error.
Insert the BLANK vial and press ZERO.
Insert the SAMPLE vial in the same orientation and press READ. Record the result in mg/L COD.

If the result exceeds the vial range, dilute the original sample with deionised water by a known factor, run a fresh digestion, and multiply by the dilution factor. Do NOT dilute an already-digested vial.
For discharge compliance, compare against the consent limit and flag any exceedance immediately per the site's escalation procedure.
Log the result, the vial range and lot, the dilution factor if any, and the sample point in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run a reagent blank with EVERY batch, using a vial from the same lot. The blank corrects for lot-to-lot reagent variation.
Run a known COD standard with each batch; recovery should be within the limits set by your QA programme.
Run a duplicate on every 10th sample. Poor duplicate agreement on wastewater usually means inadequate homogenisation, not instrument error.
Verify the reactor temperature with an independent thermometer periodically — a reactor running cool gives systematically low COD.
Verify pipette calibration on schedule and record it.
troubleshooting: Duplicates disagree badly: the sample was not homogenised, or the pipette is drawing inconsistently. Blend the sample and repeat.
All results biased low: reactor not reaching 150 °C, digestion time cut short, or reagent past expiry.
Green vial after digestion on a high-range vial: COD is above range — dilute and repeat.
Erratic readings between vials: vials not wiped clean, or inserted in different orientations. Wipe every vial and insert consistently.
Blank reads high: reagent lot issue or contaminated deionised water — check the water source.
safetyNotes: COD vials contain CONCENTRATED SULFURIC ACID, HEXAVALENT CHROMIUM, MERCURY, and SILVER. They are corrosive, toxic, and an environmental hazard.
Wear goggles, gloves, and a lab coat. Handle vials over a tray.
Vials get extremely hot on mixing and during digestion — always use the rack and heat-resistant gloves, never bare hands.
NEVER pour spent COD vials down the drain. Collect them as hazardous waste (chromium and mercury) per your site's chemical waste procedure.
If a vial breaks in the reactor, allow it to cool completely before cleaning, and treat all debris as hazardous waste.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet supplied with your vial lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: COD — Titrimetric (Closed Reflux, FAS Titration)
methodRef: Standard Methods 5220C — Closed Reflux, Titrimetric Method
frequency: Backup method when the spectrophotometer is unavailable, or for verification of the colorimetric result
holdingTime: 28 days if preserved with sulfuric acid to pH < 2 at 4 °C
equipment: COD digestion vessels and block digester (150 °C)
reagents: Potassium dichromate digestion solution (with mercuric sulfate)
Sulfuric acid reagent containing silver sulfate
Ferroin indicator solution
Standardised ferrous ammonium sulfate (FAS) titrant
Potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) standard for QC
interferences: Chloride interferes positively; mercuric sulfate in the digestion solution suppresses it up to the method's limit.
FAS titrant oxidises in air and must be re-standardised frequently — an out-of-date titrant normality is a direct multiplier on the error.
Incomplete homogenisation gives unrepresentative aliquots.
steps: Standardise the FAS titrant against the dichromate solution on the day of use, and record the normality obtained. This value goes directly into the calculation.
Homogenise/blend the sample thoroughly.
Pipette the specified sample volume into a digestion vessel, then add digestion solution and acid reagent in the order given by the method.
Prepare a blank identically, using deionised water in place of sample.
Cap tightly, invert to mix (the vessels become hot), and digest at 150 °C for 2 hours.
Cool the vessels to room temperature in a rack — do not quench.
Transfer the digestate to a flask (or titrate in the vessel per your method), add 1-2 drops of ferroin indicator, and place on a magnetic stirrer.
Titrate with standardised FAS. The colour passes from blue-green through to a sharp reddish-brown at the endpoint.
Record the FAS volume for the BLANK (A) and for the SAMPLE (B).
Enter the blank volume, sample volume, FAS normality, and sample aliquot volume into the COD calculator.
Log the result, the FAS normality used and its standardisation date, and the sample point in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Standardise FAS on each day of use — this is not optional; the titrant degrades.
Run a KHP standard of known COD with each batch; theoretical COD of KHP is 1.176 mg O2 per mg KHP.
Run a blank with every batch.
Run duplicates on every 10th sample.
troubleshooting: Endpoint is indistinct: ferroin indicator may be old, or the digestate is too dilute — check indicator and aliquot size.
Blank titration volume drifting between batches: FAS is oxidising; re-standardise.
Result disagrees with the DR6000 colorimetric result: check FAS standardisation first, then digestion temperature.
safetyNotes: Digestion solutions contain concentrated sulfuric acid, hexavalent chromium, mercury, and silver — corrosive, toxic, and environmentally hazardous.
Collect all spent digestate as hazardous waste; never pour to drain.
Vessels become extremely hot during acid addition and digestion.

title: BOD5 — 5-Day Biochemical Oxygen Demand
frequency: Per the discharge consent schedule; typically several times per week on influent and effluent
holdingTime: Begin the test within 24 h of collection (6 h preferred); store at 4 °C
equipment: 300 mL BOD bottles with ground glass stoppers and water seals
DO meter with self-stirring BOD probe (or Winkler titration apparatus)
20 L carboy for dilution water with aeration equipment
reagents: Phosphate buffer solution
Magnesium sulfate solution
Calcium chloride solution
Ferric chloride solution
Seed material (settled domestic sewage or commercial seed capsules)
Glucose-glutamic acid (GGA) standard for QC
Sodium sulfite and potassium iodide for dechlorination if required
interferences: Residual chlorine in the sample kills the microorganisms — dechlorinate before setting up.
Toxic substances (metals, high ammonia, industrial discharges) suppress the result; a suppressed BOD may look like a good result but is actually invalid.
Nitrification consumes oxygen and inflates the result unless a nitrification inhibitor is used (report as cBOD5 when inhibited).
Supersaturated or very cold samples must be brought to about 20 °C before setup, or the initial DO reading is wrong.
Dilution water that is not properly prepared or aerated invalidates the entire batch.
steps: PREPARE DILUTION WATER at least a day ahead: add the nutrient buffer solutions to deionised water, aerate to saturation, and hold at 20 °C. Its blank depletion is a direct check on its quality.
Bring samples to about 20 °C and check for residual chlorine; dechlorinate with sodium sulfite if present.

SELECT DILUTIONS to give a final DO depletion of at least 2.0 mg/L with at least 1.0 mg/L DO remaining after 5 days. Since the correct dilution is rarely known in advance, set up at least three different dilutions per sample so at least one lands in the valid window.
As a starting guide, dilute in proportion to expected strength — strong influent needs a much smaller sample fraction than final effluent.
Add seed to each bottle if the sample is not expected to contain sufficient organisms (effluent, industrial, or chlorinated samples).
Set up SEED BLANKS: bottles containing dilution water plus the same seed volume, with no sample.
Set up DILUTION WATER BLANKS: bottles with dilution water only. These must deplete less than 0.2 mg/L over 5 days or the batch is invalid.
Set up the GGA STANDARD as a check on the whole procedure.
Fill each bottle completely, insert the stopper without trapping any air bubble, and check no bubble is present — a bubble invalidates that bottle.
Measure and record the INITIAL DO (D1 for samples, B1 for seed blanks) on each bottle, or on a representative bottle per the method being followed.
Add the water seal to each bottle, cover, and place in the incubator at 20 °C in the DARK. Light promotes algal oxygen production and ruins results.
After exactly 5 days (±2 hours), measure and record the FINAL DO (D2 and B2).
VALIDATE EACH BOTTLE before using it: depletion must be at least 2.0 mg/L AND at least 1.0 mg/L DO must remain. Discard bottles that fail either criterion and use one that passes.
Enter D1, D2, B1, B2, the seed correction factor, and the decimal dilution fraction into the BOD5 calculator.
Where several dilutions are valid, average their results per the method's rules.
Use the influent BOD together with plant flow, aeration volume, and MLVSS in the F/M Ratio calculator for process control.
Log the result, all dilutions used, which bottles were valid, and the blank/GGA performance in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Dilution water blank must deplete less than 0.2 mg/L over 5 days — if it exceeds this, the whole batch is suspect.
GGA standard should recover 198 ± 30.5 mg/L (the Standard Methods acceptance window); a failing GGA indicates a problem with seed, dilution water, or technique.
Run duplicates and track precision over time.
Verify incubator temperature daily and record it.
Verify DO meter calibration before each reading session.
troubleshooting: All bottles depleted to zero: sample was under-diluted. Set up more dilutions covering weaker fractions.
No measurable depletion: sample over-diluted, or the sample is toxic/inhibited, or chlorine was not fully removed.
GGA fails low: seed inactive or dilution water nutrient-deficient.
Result is much lower than COD would suggest: suspect toxicity or inhibition in the sample.
Erratic results across duplicates: air bubbles in bottles, or inconsistent DO probe technique.
safetyNotes: Wastewater samples are a biohazard — wear gloves, avoid aerosols, and wash hands thoroughly afterwards.
Do not mouth-pipette anything.
Handle glass BOD bottles carefully; stoppers can jam and bottles crack under pressure.

title: Ammonia Nitrogen — Hach Salicylate (DR6000)
hachMethod: Method 8155 — Salicylate, powder pillows or TNTplus vials
range: 0.01 – 0.50 mg/L NH3-N (low range); higher ranges available via TNTplus vials
wavelength: 655 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: Daily on effluent for consent monitoring; more often during nitrification upsets
holdingTime: 28 days if preserved with sulfuric acid to pH < 2 at 4 °C; otherwise analyse within 24 h
equipment: Matched sample cells or TNTplus vial adapter
reagents: Ammonia salicylate reagent
Ammonia cyanurate reagent
Deionised, ammonia-free water for blank and dilution
interferences: Ammonia contamination is everywhere in a lab — cleaning products, smoking, and even breath affect low-level results. Keep ammonia work away from cleaning chemicals.
Turbidity and colour interfere; filter turbid samples.
High concentrations of calcium, magnesium, or iron can cause precipitation — the method includes conditioning steps to manage this.
The green colour continues developing; read within the window the method specifies.
steps: Collect the sample and, if it will not be analysed immediately, preserve with sulfuric acid to pH < 2 and refrigerate.
Filter the sample if it is visibly turbid.
Select the stored program for ammonia nitrogen by the salicylate method (Hach Method 8155) on the DR6000, matching the reagent format in use (powder pillow or TNTplus).
DILUTE if the sample is expected above range — untreated influent typically needs substantial dilution. Use ammonia-free deionised water and record the factor.
PREPARE THE BLANK using ammonia-free deionised water in place of sample, treated with the same reagents.
PREPARE THE SAMPLE: add the salicylate reagent, then the cyanurate reagent, in the order and quantities specified, swirling to dissolve after each.
Start the 20-minute instrument timer. A green colour develops in proportion to ammonia present.
When the timer expires, wipe both cells, zero on the blank, then read the sample.
Multiply by the dilution factor if the sample was diluted, and record both the raw and corrected values.

Interpret for process control: ammonia in final effluent indicates incomplete nitrification. Check dissolved oxygen in the aeration basin, sludge age (SRT), temperature, and pH — nitrifiers are slow-growing and are the first organisms lost when SRT drops or DO is inadequate.
Log the result, the sample point, and the associated DO/SRT data in the Logbook so the process picture stays connected.
qualityControl: Run a reagent blank with every batch using ammonia-free water.
Verify against an ammonia standard on the QA schedule.
Run duplicates on every 10th sample.
Run a spiked sample periodically to check for matrix interference in your effluent.
troubleshooting: Blank reads high: ammonia contamination in the deionised water, glassware, or laboratory air. Isolate ammonia work from cleaning chemicals.
Result over range: dilute with ammonia-free water and repeat.
Colour weak on a known-positive sample: reagents added out of order or expired.
Poor duplicates: turbidity — filter the sample before analysis.
safetyNotes: Salicylate and cyanurate reagents are irritants; cyanurate reagent is harmful if ingested.
Wastewater samples are a biohazard — gloves and hand washing required.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Nitrate — Hach Cadmium Reduction (DR6000)
hachMethod: Method 8039 — NitraVer 5 cadmium reduction, high range
reactionTime: 1 minute vigorous mixing, then 5 minute reaction
frequency: Daily on effluent where total nitrogen is consented; during denitrification troubleshooting
holdingTime: 48 h at 4 °C unpreserved; 28 days if acid preserved to pH < 2
reagents: NitraVer 5 Nitrate Reagent powder pillows
Deionised water for blank and dilution
interferences: The mixing step is unusually critical for this method — the cadmium must be agitated vigorously for the full period or results are low and irreproducible.
Strong oxidising and reducing substances interfere.
High chloride biases results low; high iron interferes.
Undissolved reagent is normal and does not affect the reading, but incomplete mixing does.
steps: Collect the sample and filter if visibly turbid.
Select the stored program for nitrate by cadmium reduction (Hach Method 8039) on the DR6000.
PREPARE THE BLANK: fill a clean cell to the 10 mL mark with untreated sample.
PREPARE THE SAMPLE: fill the second matched cell to the 10 mL mark and add one NitraVer 5 powder pillow.
Cap and SHAKE VIGOROUSLY for the full 1 minute specified. This is the step most often shortened, and shortening it gives low results. Use the instrument timer, not judgement.
Start the 5-minute reaction timer and let the sample stand undisturbed. An amber colour develops if nitrate is present.
When the timer expires, wipe both cells, zero on the blank, then read the sample within the method's reading window — the colour is not stable indefinitely.
Multiply by any dilution factor applied and record both values.

Interpret for process control: nitrate in effluent means nitrification is working but denitrification is not removing it. Check anoxic zone conditions, internal recycle rate, and whether sufficient carbon is available for denitrifiers.
Consider nitrate together with ammonia: high ammonia and low nitrate means nitrification is failing; low ammonia and high nitrate means nitrification works but denitrification is limited.
Log the result alongside the ammonia result and process conditions in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run a blank with each batch.
Verify against a nitrate standard on the QA schedule — this method's accuracy is technique-sensitive, so standard checks matter more than usual.
Run duplicates on every 10th sample; poor agreement usually means inconsistent shaking.
Record reagent lot and expiry.
troubleshooting: Results low and variable: insufficient or inconsistent shaking during the reduction step. Time it and shake vigorously.
Result over range: dilute and repeat.
Colour fading before reading: read promptly once the reaction timer expires.
safetyNotes: NitraVer 5 CONTAINS CADMIUM, which is toxic and an environmental hazard.
Collect all spent samples and reagent as hazardous waste — never pour cadmium-containing waste down the drain.
Avoid all skin contact and do not inhale the powder.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Phosphorus, Total — Hach Acid Persulfate Digestion (DR6000)
methodRef: Hach Method 8190 — Acid Persulfate Digestion followed by PhosVer 3 (Method 8048)
instrument: Hach DR6000 Spectrophotometer with DRB200 reactor
hachMethod: Method 8190 — Total phosphorus, acid persulfate digestion
range: 0.06 – 3.50 mg/L PO4 (as measured after digestion); dilute higher samples
reactionTime: 30 minutes digestion at 150 °C, then 2 minutes colour development
wavelength: 880 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: Per the discharge consent schedule; commonly weekly to daily on final effluent
holdingTime: 28 days if preserved with sulfuric acid to pH < 2 at 4 °C
equipment: Test tube rack and heat-resistant gloves
reagents: Potassium persulfate powder pillows for phosphonate
Sodium hydroxide solution 1.54 N
PhosVer 3 phosphate powder pillows
Deionised water for blank and dilution
interferences: Phosphate-containing detergents contaminate glassware — never use them for phosphorus work.
Incomplete digestion under-reports total phosphorus, since organic and condensed phosphates are not converted to orthophosphate.
Turbidity and colour interfere with the final reading.
Neutralisation after digestion must be correct, or colour development is affected.
steps: Preheat the DRB200 reactor to 150 °C.
Collect and homogenise the sample. Total phosphorus includes particulate forms, so the aliquot must be representative.
Pipette the specified sample volume into a digestion vial, and prepare a blank identically with deionised water.
Add the potassium persulfate reagent to each vial and cap tightly. Invert to dissolve.
Digest at 150 °C for 30 minutes. This step converts organic and condensed phosphates to orthophosphate — skipping or shortening it means you are measuring only reactive phosphorus, not total.
Cool the vials to room temperature in a rack. Do not quench.
Add sodium hydroxide solution to neutralise, per the method's specified volume.
Select the stored program for total phosphorus (Hach Method 8190) on the DR6000.
Add the PhosVer 3 reagent to each vial and start the 2-minute colour development timer.
Wipe both vials, zero on the blank, and read the sample. Record the result.
Apply any dilution factor and record both the raw and corrected results.
Compare to the discharge consent limit. If phosphorus removal is chemical, review the coagulant dose; if biological, review the anaerobic zone conditions.
Log the result, digestion batch, and any dosing change in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Run a digested blank with every batch — the blank must go through the full digestion, not just the colour step.
Verify against a phosphorus standard taken through the complete digestion procedure; this checks digestion efficiency, not just colour development.
Run duplicates on every 10th sample.
Verify reactor temperature periodically.
troubleshooting: Total phosphorus result equal to reactive phosphorus: digestion is not working — check reactor temperature and persulfate reagent age.
High blank: phosphate contamination from glassware or detergent.
Poor duplicates: sample not homogenised, so particulate phosphorus is unevenly sampled.
safetyNotes: Persulfate is a strong oxidiser; sodium hydroxide is caustic. Both require gloves and eye protection.
Vials are extremely hot after digestion — use the rack and heat-resistant gloves.
Wastewater samples are a biohazard.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet for your reagent lot; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: Suspended Solids — Hach Photometric (DR6000)
methodRef: Hach Method 8006 — Photometric suspended solids (screening method)
wavelength: 810 nm (set automatically by the stored program)
frequency: As a rapid process check through the shift; the gravimetric method is required for compliance reporting
holdingTime: Analyse immediately — solids settle and the sample changes rapidly
reagents: Deionised water for blank
interferences: This is a light-scattering measurement, so particle size and colour strongly affect it. Results are NOT directly comparable to gravimetric TSS unless correlated for your specific sample matrix.
Settling during the measurement gives a falling reading — read immediately after mixing.
Air bubbles read as solids.
Coloured samples bias the result.
steps: Understand the method's role first: this is a fast screening tool for process control. For discharge compliance reporting, use the gravimetric MLSS/TSS procedure instead.
Blend the sample at high speed for the period specified by the method to break up flocs to a consistent particle size — this step is what makes results reproducible.
Let the blended sample stand briefly to release air bubbles introduced by blending.
Select the stored program for suspended solids (Hach Method 8006) on the DR6000.
PREPARE THE BLANK: fill a clean cell to the 10 mL mark with deionised water. Wipe, insert, and press ZERO.
Swirl the blended sample to re-suspend, then immediately fill the second matched cell to the 10 mL mark.
Wipe the cell and insert it promptly — every second of delay lets solids settle and lowers the reading.
Press READ and record the result in mg/L TSS.

CORRELATE before relying on the numbers: run parallel photometric and gravimetric determinations on your own samples to establish the relationship for your plant, and note that correlation in the Logbook.
Use for rapid checks — mixed liquor trends through a shift, clarifier carryover, or confirming a process change — and confirm anything significant gravimetrically.
Log the result, noting clearly that it is the photometric screening method rather than gravimetric.
qualityControl: Establish and periodically re-verify a correlation against the gravimetric method for your plant's sample matrix.
Run duplicates; poor agreement means inconsistent blending or settling delay.
Use deionised water blanks to confirm the instrument zero.
Never report a photometric result as a gravimetric one for compliance purposes.
troubleshooting: Reading falls while the cell sits in the instrument: solids settling — mix and read faster.
Photometric and gravimetric results diverge over time: the floc character has changed; re-establish the correlation.
Erratic results: inconsistent blending time or air bubbles.
safetyNotes: Wastewater samples are a biohazard — wear gloves, avoid aerosols (especially when blending), and wash hands afterwards.
Blend with the lid secured to avoid spraying sample.
The definitive reference is the Hach method sheet; this SOP is a bench summary.

title: MLSS / MLVSS — Gravimetric Method
methodRef: Standard Methods 2540 D (TSS) and 2540 E (volatile solids)
frequency: Daily on mixed liquor and RAS; MLVSS weekly or per process control needs
holdingTime: Analyse within 24 h; refrigerate at 4 °C if held
equipment: Glass fibre filter discs (1.5 µm nominal, e.g. Whatman 934-AH)
Graduated cylinder for accurate sample volume
reagents: Deionised water for rinsing
interferences: A non-representative sample is the main error — mixed liquor settles within seconds, so the aliquot must be taken while actively mixing.
Failure to reach constant mass leaves residual moisture and biases results high.
Handling filters with bare fingers adds mass; always use forceps.
Excessive sample volume clogs the filter and extends filtration time, allowing losses.
Static electricity on dry filters affects weighing on sensitive balances.
steps: PREPARE FILTERS: place a glass fibre filter on the filtration apparatus, apply vacuum, and rinse with three successive volumes of deionised water to remove loose fibres.
Transfer the filter to a weighing dish and dry at 103-105 °C for at least 1 hour.
Cool in a desiccator to room temperature and weigh. Repeat the drying and weighing cycle until constant mass is reached (successive weights within 0.5 mg). Record this TARE mass.
For MLVSS work, ignite the tared filter at 550 °C for 15-20 minutes first, then re-cool and re-weigh, so the tare already accounts for ignition losses in the filter itself.
COLLECT THE SAMPLE while the mixed liquor is actively mixing. Take the aliquot immediately — do not let the sample stand.
Choose a sample volume that yields 2.5 to 200 mg of residue. For typical mixed liquor, 25-50 mL is usual; too much clogs the filter.
Swirl the sample immediately before pouring, and measure the volume accurately with a graduated cylinder.
Filter the measured sample under vacuum, then rinse the cylinder and filter with three small volumes of deionised water to transfer all solids and wash out dissolved salts.
Continue the vacuum for about 3 minutes after filtration completes to remove excess water.
Transfer the filter carefully to the weighing dish with forceps and dry at 103-105 °C for at least 1 hour.
Cool in a desiccator and weigh promptly. Repeat drying/cooling/weighing to constant mass. Record as FILTER + DRIED RESIDUE.
FOR MLVSS: ignite the same filter and residue at 550 °C for 15-20 minutes. Volatile (organic) matter burns off; inert matter remains.
Cool the ignited filter briefly in air, then in a desiccator to room temperature, and weigh promptly. Record as FILTER + RESIDUE AFTER IGNITION.
Enter the tare mass, dried mass, ignited mass (if measured), and sample volume into the MLSS / MLVSS calculator.
Use the MLSS result in the SVI calculator (with the settleability test) and the Sludge Age calculator, and the MLVSS result in the F/M Ratio calculator.

Log MLSS, MLVSS, the MLVSS/MLSS ratio, and the sample point in the Logbook. The ratio typically runs around 0.7-0.8 in conventional activated sludge; a falling ratio indicates accumulating inert material.
qualityControl: Run duplicates on every 10th sample; agreement should be within about 5 %.
Verify oven and furnace temperatures with independent thermometers periodically.
Verify balance calibration with check weights before each weighing session.
Confirm constant mass is genuinely reached rather than assumed — this is the most common shortcut and it biases results.
Keep desiccant active; exhausted desiccant lets samples regain moisture during cooling.
troubleshooting: Results scattered between duplicates: sample not taken while mixing, or volumes measured imprecisely.
Filtration extremely slow: sample volume too large, or filter blinded by fine solids — use a smaller volume.
Mass keeps changing between weighings: incomplete drying or exhausted desiccant.
MLVSS higher than MLSS (impossible): weighing or recording error — check the tare and ignition masses.
Sudden MLSS shift with no operational change: verify the sample point and that the sample was taken from a mixed zone.
safetyNotes: The muffle furnace operates at 550 °C — use long tongs, heat-resistant gloves, and a face shield, and never place hot items on flammable surfaces.
Allow ignited filters to cool in air briefly before placing them in a desiccator, or the desiccator lid can be blown off.
Wastewater samples are a biohazard — gloves and hand washing required.
Never place a hot dish on the analytical balance.

title: Settleability and Sludge Volume Index (SVI)
methodRef: Standard Methods 2710D (settled sludge volume) / 2710 SVI calculation
frequency: Daily, at the same time each day — consistency of timing is what makes the trend meaningful
holdingTime: Start the test immediately after collection; sludge character changes within minutes
equipment: 1 litre graduated cylinder or Mallory settleometer
Sample container for the parallel MLSS determination
interferences: Temperature affects settling rate — record it, and be cautious comparing results across seasons.
Vibration or draughts disturb settling and give inconsistent results; place the cylinder somewhere stable.
Delays between collection and starting the test change the result.
A cylinder of different diameter gives different results — always use the same vessel.
steps: Collect a fresh, well-mixed mixed liquor sample from the aeration basin outlet (or the site's designated point), while the basin is mixing.
Start the test immediately. Fill the 1 litre cylinder to the mark, pouring gently to avoid shearing the floc.
Start the timer as soon as the cylinder is filled, and place it where it will not be disturbed or heated by sunlight.
Record the sludge interface level at intervals — 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 minutes. The shape of the settling curve is far more informative than the 30-minute value alone.
Observe and note the settling character: a well-settling sludge forms a distinct, sharp interface and compacts cleanly, leaving a clear supernatant.
Note the supernatant clarity and whether any pin floc, straggler floc, or floating sludge is present.
At exactly 30 minutes, record the settled sludge volume (SSV30) in mL/L.
Determine MLSS on a parallel sample of the same mixed liquor using the gravimetric MLSS procedure.
Enter SSV30 and MLSS into the SVI calculator.

INTERPRET the SVI: values around 80-150 mL/g generally indicate good settling. Above roughly 150 mL/g suggests bulking (often filamentous); well below 80 mL/g suggests a dense, possibly old or pin-floc sludge that may settle fast but leave a turbid supernatant.

If SVI is rising, look at the settling curve and supernatant together — slow settling with a distinct interface points toward filamentous bulking, while a cloudy supernatant with fast settling points toward floc deflocculation or excessive sludge age.
Where bulking is suspected, examine the sludge microscopically for filaments before making large process changes.
Log SSV30, MLSS, calculated SVI, temperature, settling observations, and supernatant clarity in the Logbook. Trend SVI daily — the direction of travel matters more than any single value.
qualityControl: Run the test at the same time each day from the same sample point with the same vessel.
Record temperature with every test.
Pair every SVI with an MLSS from the same sample — an SVI calculated from a stale MLSS is meaningless.
Note any deviation from routine (basin upset, storm flow, chemical dosing change) alongside the result.
troubleshooting: Sludge will not settle at all: severe bulking, or a toxic/shock load has deflocculated the sludge.
Sludge rises after initially settling: denitrification in the cylinder producing nitrogen bubbles — this predicts rising sludge in the clarifier.
Interface indistinct: dispersed growth or deflocculation; check for toxicity, low DO, or very low sludge age.
SVI jumps day to day with no process change: check sampling consistency (point, time, vessel) before suspecting the process.
safetyNotes: Wastewater is a biohazard — gloves, no aerosols, wash hands after handling.
Handle 1 L glass cylinders carefully; they are top-heavy when full.

title: Dissolved Oxygen — Membrane Electrode / Optical Method
frequency: Continuous on-line in aeration basins where fitted, plus bench/field verification per shift
holdingTime: MEASURE IN SITU — DO changes immediately on sampling due to atmospheric exchange and ongoing biological activity
equipment: DO meter with membrane or optical (luminescent) probe
Probe with stirring capability, or a means of maintaining flow across the membrane
Barometer or local barometric pressure reading
reagents: Membrane and electrolyte replacement kit (membrane probes)
Zero-DO solution (sodium sulfite) for zero verification
interferences: Membrane probes CONSUME oxygen at the membrane, so they require continuous flow or stirring — a stagnant reading falls continuously and reads falsely low. This is the most common DO measurement error.
A fouled, wrinkled, or damaged membrane gives slow, low, and drifting readings.
Temperature and barometric pressure both affect oxygen saturation and must be accounted for.
Biological activity in a grab sample continues consuming oxygen, so the result falls with time.
Optical probes are less flow-sensitive but their sensing caps age and need replacement on schedule.
steps: Inspect the probe. For a membrane probe, check the membrane is smooth, intact, and free of bubbles or fouling; replace membrane and electrolyte per schedule. For an optical probe, check the sensing cap is clean and within its service life.

CALIBRATE in water-saturated air: place the probe in the calibration sleeve with a damp sponge, keeping the sensor out of direct contact with water, and allow the temperature and reading to stabilise fully before accepting.
Enter or confirm the local barometric pressure (or altitude) if the meter requires it — an incorrect pressure shifts every subsequent reading.
Verify the zero point with a sodium sulfite solution at the frequency your QA programme requires.
MEASURE IN SITU wherever possible. Lower the probe directly into the aeration basin at the standard depth and location used for trending.
Ensure adequate flow across the sensor: use the probe's stirrer, or move the probe steadily through the water. For a membrane probe, a still reading is not a valid reading.
Allow the reading to stabilise fully — this can take a minute or more from a large temperature change — then record DO in mg/L and the temperature.
Take readings at several points across the basin, not just one. DO gradients across an aeration basin are normal and informative; a single point can hide both dead zones and over-aerated zones.

Enter the temperature, measured DO, and barometric pressure correction into the DO % Saturation calculator to convert to percent saturation, which is more comparable across temperatures than raw mg/L.

INTERPRET for process control: conventional activated sludge typically targets around 1.5-2.0 mg/L in the aeration basin. Consistently below about 0.5 mg/L risks filamentous bulking and failed nitrification; consistently high wastes a great deal of blower energy and can break up floc.
Cross-check against ammonia results — nitrification failing while DO looks adequate points to sludge age or toxicity rather than aeration.
Rinse the probe with clean water after use and store per the manufacturer's instructions (membrane probes are stored wet).
Log DO readings by location, temperature, percent saturation, and blower/aeration settings in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Calibrate daily before the first reading and record the calibration.
Verify zero with sodium sulfite on the QA schedule.
Compare the hand-held reading against the on-line basin instrument at the same point and time; a persistent offset means one of them needs attention.
Track membrane/cap replacement dates — performance degrades gradually and is easy to miss.
Record barometric pressure used for calibration.
troubleshooting: Reading falls steadily while the probe sits in the sample: insufficient flow across a membrane probe. Stir or move the probe.
Slow response and low readings: fouled or damaged membrane, or depleted electrolyte — service the probe.
Calibration will not hold: membrane, electrolyte, or sensing cap at end of life.
Field and on-line readings disagree: verify both calibrations and confirm the hand-held probe is at the same depth and location as the installed sensor.
DO reads high but the process behaves as if oxygen-limited: check for short-circuiting or dead zones — measure at multiple points.
safetyNotes: Working at basin edges is a drowning and fall hazard — use the site's fall protection, work with a colleague, and never lean over a handrail.
Wastewater is a biohazard; wear gloves and wash hands after handling probes.
Sodium sulfite zero solution is an irritant.

title: WAS / RAS Sampling Procedure
frequency: Daily, at a consistent time, matched to the mixed liquor sampling round
holdingTime: Analyse within 24 h at 4 °C; settleability and DO must be done immediately
interferences: Sampling from a stagnant line gives sludge that has been sitting, not the sludge currently being pumped.
Sludge is highly non-homogeneous; a single grab from a poorly mixed point is not representative.
Sampling at inconsistent times relative to the wasting cycle produces trends that reflect the sampling, not the process.
steps: Identify the correct sample point from the plant flow diagram — RAS from the return line, WAS from the wasting line. Confirm you are sampling the stream you intend.
Confirm the relevant pump is RUNNING before sampling. Sampling a WAS line while the wasting pump is off gives a stale, unrepresentative sample.
Flush the sample tap for long enough to clear the line of standing material before collecting.
Collect into a clean, clearly labelled container. Label it at the moment of collection — WAS and RAS samples look identical.
Fill the container leaving a little headspace so it can be mixed before subsampling.
Record the time, the pump running status, and the current wasting rate at the moment of sampling — the result cannot be interpreted without the wasting rate.
Deliver to the bench promptly and mix thoroughly immediately before taking any subsample.
Run the required analyses: TSS/VSS by the gravimetric procedure, and settleability where applicable.
Use the WAS TSS concentration and the wasting flow rate to calculate the mass of solids wasted per day in kg/day, and enter it into the Sludge Age (SRT) calculator.

Cross-check the SRT result against the site's target sludge age. SRT is the single most important activated sludge control parameter — nitrification in particular depends on holding enough sludge age at the current temperature.
Log the WAS/RAS concentrations, wasting rate, calculated SRT, and any wasting adjustment in the Logbook.
qualityControl: Sample at the same time each day relative to the wasting cycle.
Confirm and record pump running status with every sample.
Run duplicates periodically; sludge heterogeneity means duplicates are less repeatable than clear-water analyses.
Reconcile calculated solids inventory against the measured MLSS trend — if SRT says one thing and MLSS trend says another, check the wasting flow measurement.
troubleshooting: WAS concentration much lower than RAS: the wasting line may be drawing from the wrong point, or the pump was off during sampling.
SRT calculation gives an implausible value: check the wasting flow measurement first, since flow error usually dominates.
Day-to-day SRT swings with steady operation: inconsistent sampling time relative to intermittent wasting — sample consistently or use a flow-proportional composite.
RAS concentration falling: possible clarifier sludge blanket issue or excessive return rate diluting the sludge.
safetyNotes: Activated sludge is a biohazard — wear gloves and eye protection, avoid aerosols and splashing, and wash hands thoroughly.
Sample points near moving pumps and valves present mechanical hazards; follow lockout requirements before opening anything beyond a sample tap.
Watch for slip hazards around sludge sample points.
